opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is that it needs to become a real community rather than a handful of scattered groups who each discovered, somewhat independently, that you can treat neural network weights as a data modality. For a long time people were doing related things under different names, like hypernetworks, model zoos, learned optimizers, implicit neural representations, model merging and pruning, and they weren't necessarily talking to each other. One of the most useful things we can do is bring those threads together, with workshops, shared vocabulary and joint problem statements, so people realize they're working on the same underlying question: what is the structure of the space of trained models, and how can we learn on it?

Second, we need shared infrastructure, and I'd put datasets at the top of that list. In computer vision ImageNet gave everyone a common playing field. For weight space learning that means model zoos: large, well-documented populations of trained networks with varied architectures, seeds, hyperparameters and training trajectories, released openly so results are comparable. We've tried to contribute to that, but it has to be a community effort, because generating these populations is expensive and the design choices really matter. If every paper trains its own little zoo, you can't tell whether a method works or just fits a quirk of how that zoo was made.

Third, benchmarks and evaluation protocols. What does it mean to have a good representation of a model? Can you predict its accuracy or generalization gap, detect a backdoor, tell which data it was trained on, generate new weights that work out of the box? We need agreed-upon tasks so progress can be measured rather than just claimed.

Then there are the hard technical questions that should drive the research agenda. Symmetries are a big one: permutation symmetries, scaling symmetries, the fact that many different weight configurations implement the same function. Equivariant architectures for weights have made great progress, but we're still early. Scale is another: most work so far has been on relatively small networks, and the real test is whether these ideas carry over to foundation-model-sized weights, maybe by working on subsets of the weights, on adapters like LoRA, or with tokenization schemes that handle very large parameter vectors. And heterogeneity matters: we want methods that work across architectures, not just within one fixed family.

Finally, I'd like the community to keep one eye on applications. Huggingface and similar hubs hold an enormous, mostly unexploited population of trained models. If we can learn from that population, we can search it, audit it, reuse it, and even generate new models instead of training from scratch, and that has real implications for efficiency, sustainability, and safety. That's what will make the field matter beyond being an interesting academic niche.

So: build bridges between subcommunities, invest in open model zoos and benchmarks, take the fundamental questions about symmetry and scale seriously, and connect it all to the very practical reality that we now live in a world full of trained models. If we do that, I think weight space learning can become a genuine pillar of machine learning research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that weight space learning is still a very young field, and right now it's a bit fragmented. You have people coming from the model zoo side, people coming from hypernetworks, people doing neural functionals and permutation equivariance, people doing model merging and task arithmetic, and often they don't really talk to each other or even realize they're working on the same underlying problem, which is: treat the trained weights of a neural network as a data modality and learn on top of that.

So the first thing I'd like to see is that we come together as a community and agree on a shared vocabulary and shared benchmarks. In computer vision we had ImageNet, in NLP you had GLUE and so on, and that's what allowed people to compare methods and actually measure progress. In weight space we don't really have that yet. We have individual model zoos, including our own, but they are built with different architectures, different training regimes, different documentation, and it's hard to say whether method A is better than method B or whether it just saw a nicer population of models. So large, well-documented, diverse populations of models, where you know the hyperparameters, the data, the training trajectory, and standardized downstream tasks, like predicting accuracy, predicting the training data properties, detecting backdoors, generating new models, that is infrastructure the community needs.

The second thing is the theory side. We need to understand the structure of weight space much better. The symmetries, permutation and scaling, we understand reasonably well now, but what about the geometry across architectures, across sizes, across different pretraining data? If we want to go from small CNNs in a model zoo to actual foundation models, we need methods that scale, and we need a theoretical understanding of what is actually preserved and what is noise.

And the third thing, honestly, is to connect to problems people care about. There is a huge amount of trained models out there, on Hugging Face alone, and almost nobody looks at them as data. If we can show that weight space learning helps with model auditing, with detecting if a model was trained on certain data, with transferring knowledge between models without retraining, or with generating good initializations so you save compute, then the community will grow by itself because the applications pull it along.

So, short version: shared benchmarks and model zoos, better theory, and real applications. And more collaboration between these subcommunities, because right now a lot of the ideas are being reinvented in parallel.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to build a community that connects people who are looking at neural network weights from different perspectives. Some are interested in understanding trained models, others in predicting their properties, and others in generating new models. There are common questions underneath those applications: How do we represent a neural network? How do we account for symmetries? And what can we learn across networks with different architectures?

A practical step is to develop shared datasets and benchmarks. If we want to learn from populations of models, we need collections with enough diversity to test whether a method generalizes. Does it work on a new training run, a new task, or a new architecture? Those are quite different claims, and we should be precise about them.

And I would like to see more exchange between the theoretical and empirical work. We need methods that do useful things, but also a better understanding of why they work and what information the weights actually contain. Shared resources and a place to discuss those questions would help the field develop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to bring together people who are currently looking at this from different perspectives. Some are studying the geometry of neural networks, some are working on model merging, and others are trying to learn representations of the weights themselves. There are a lot of shared questions there, and it would be valuable to build a community around those questions.

One practical step is to have shared datasets of trained models, together with good documentation of how they were trained. If we want to learn across neural networks, we need to understand what variation we’re actually capturing. Is it the task? The architecture? Or simply the random seed and the training procedure? And we need benchmarks that test whether what we learn transfers beyond the collection of models we started with.

For me, the exciting direction is to connect that understanding to something useful. Can we use a representation in weight space to help adapt a model, predict its behavior, or initialize a new model more effectively? Having common resources and clear problems would let more people contribute and help us understand which ideas really generalize.
